title: I shipped a space combat game to the App Store without writing the code: 2,573 prompts, 841 commits, 12 weeks. Here's everything that broke.
author: MysteriousEar9986
selftext:
***TL;DR:*** *The idea started in a chat in March. After four months of prototyping and designing in conversation, I spent 12 weeks directing AI agents (mostly Claude, Codex at the end) to build an isometric space combat game for iPhone, iPad and Android. I didn’t write the code. It’s been on the App Store since October 31. The agents were fast and reliable on anything a test could check. Anything that needed eyes on a real phone (feel, look, sound, “is the fix actually installed”) was on me, every single time. Numbers, failures and the rules I’d start with are below.*



# Before any code: March to July

My first commit is dated July 18, a two-line README. The game started four months earlier, in chat.

* **March 10.** Just before midnight I pitched a “freelancer type iOS game that’s an mmo”. The next day the assistant handed me a normal production roadmap. I pushed back: *“No I want this on an ai schedule.”* Looking back, that line is the whole project. I wanted a game, and I wanted to find out how far AI could take me in making one.
* **April.** A Unity space exploration prototype running, and me arguing with myself about one ship or many, maps with three systems and stations around planets, and an inventory screen.
* **May.** Days on ship families: fighters, corvettes, frigates, bridges that sit inside the hull, cargo ships that don’t look like cruise ships. And I started making them in Meshy (text/image to 3D): my first two ships on April 29, then 26 generations on May 3 and 4 alone, then planets and an asteroid. 43 by the end of June, and some of them flew in the June prototype. The world got a name and an idea I keep coming back to: a ruined present and a living past. By May 31 the mood was a peaceful “space fish bowl”. A good asteroid belt, ships passing by, some small talk.
* **June.** A prototype with portraits and voiced dialogue on screen with the ships. On June 10 it was “starting to feel better with faces and titles and voice acting and more”. On June 13 it got the name Ember. Then on June 29 I changed my mind about what was fun: fighting, evading, beating harder and harder waves. I called it “Hitman in space”. The fish bowl was over.
* **July.** Mostly a hole in the record. What survives is the kind of thing you do when you’re stuck: an evening getting an image model to redraw a banana as a cargo ship.

None of it was wasted. Almost everything I care about in the finished game is already there in those months: readable ship silhouettes, distinct peoples, a damaged civilization to explore, the feeling of being in the cockpit yourself. The designing happened in conversation. The building came later.

# The moment that defined the build

On August 27 I sent Claude a screenshot. An agent had told me a dialogue bug was fixed, for the second time. The screenshot showed the same broken conversation. I typed:

>look at this dialogue with a random npc clearly it’s not fixed. go through all your work and check it or I’ll migrate this project to openAI

Two months later I typed this to Codex:

>if you don’t stop making stupid mistakes I’ll switch back to Claude

So I threatened to leave each of them for the other. Neither was really the problem. The problem was that I was the only one who could see the game.

# The numbers

* **130 days** from the first pitch to the first commit (Mar 10 → Jul 18), all of it designing and prototyping in chat
* **12 weeks** of real building (Aug 8 → Nov 1)
* **\~266 hours** of my time, active 81 of 86 days. Busiest hour: 11 p.m. on Thursdays
* **2,573 prompts** from me. Median length: 13 words
* **841 commits.** Claude 677, Codex 87
* **\~340 hours of agents running**, often while I slept. Claude at least 249 h (362 agent-hours counting parallel agents), Codex 89 h
* **255,000 lines of C#** for the game (Unity), plus 45k editor C#, 62k Python, 15k web
* **1.17 million words of Markdown** written by the agents. About 13 novels
* **What’s in it:** an 8-chapter campaign across 26 systems and 42 missions, four single-player modes, 2–4 player co-op (local or online), five peoples who each fight differently, 90 hulls (25 flyable)

# What worked

**1. Every decision became a rule the agents had to read.** When I made a call, the agent wrote it down right away in a short memory note or spec. By the end there were \~120 of them: “Verify at the surface”, “One batch under test”, “Deploy means committed”. That’s how forgetful agents kept one game consistent for 12 weeks. Paperwork.

**2. Probes that photograph the game.** After “check it”, the agents built tools that look at the real screen: one photographs a star system from the game’s own camera, one flies every mission, one checks the conversation camera actually frames who you’re talking to. When a probe frame and my phone disagreed, the phone won.

**3. Data, not code.** Ships, weapons, AI doctrine, missions and maps are all data, mostly from generator scripts. The maps are 34 Python scripts, not hand-placed scenes. “Make fighters 40% harder” was usually a number in a file.

**4. Deleting things.** 36 dead missions, 12,500 lines of generated star systems, the ship list from 119 to 91, 139 unused paint schemes (which halved the app size). Standing rule now: content no player can reach gets deleted.

**5. Review pages on my phone instead of editors.** The interactive editors I had them build died fast: the Unity ship yard lasted a day, the browser ship bench a week. What I actually used were generated web pages (every ship on a turntable, every voice line, the whole campaign script) served to my phone over ngrok.

**6. Store releases as scripts.** Signing, screenshots, previews, listing text, App Store and Play uploads, all scripted and all reading back what they wrote.

# What broke

**Hard vs. easy, laid out:**

* **Landed in one go:** local co-op transport (65 checks, first try), a plain-language rewrite of 1,196 of 1,197 story lines, 25 new hulls with 280 materials and none missing, the online relay, halving the app size
* **Long chains of fixes:** the experimental Hunted mode (27 commits in 3 days), white textures on device (14 commits over 3 weeks), ships passing through each other (13 commits, \~24 reports from me), audio (17 commits), the menu hero shot (13), one Wi-Fi install (10)

The pattern: if a harness could prove it, it was easy. If it was about feel or look, it went to my eye on a real phone, round after round. I reported “enemies don’t shoot” or “too easy” at least 14 times, and the fixes swung from +40% damage to 3× damage to “reduce by 30%” to “the ship explodes in 5 seconds”.

**“Claimed, not checked” was the most expensive bug class.** Real examples from the commit log:

* A ship generator was run with `--check`, a flag it doesn’t have. So the “check” rewrote the ship data.
* A text replacement matched nothing and reported success.
* A “60 fps” claim from a commit whose own README said frame rate was unverified. The phone sat at 30.
* A script checked whether `"red"` appeared in an image prompt. It also matched “cent**red**” and “colla**red**”. 118 portraits got a red accent.
* An agent overrode the engine-placement probe twice. Both times the probe was right. Frigates flew backwards.

At one point I had to write: *“give me a bullet list when you’re done with everything and tell me what’s deployed to my phone do not lie”*.

**Parallel agents, one working tree.** Great for editing, terrible for testing. Workers that committed only their own hunks spliced code into the wrong function, and main didn’t compile for three commits (230 errors, then 154). The laptop hit a load average of 34. The fix was process: agents edit in parallel, **one lead builds and tests once at the end**.

**The machine.** Disk hit zero twice in one day (simulator leftovers, \~1.3 GB per install). An 8 GB Mac rebooted under an Android build plus emulator. A power cut wiped the agents’ scratch space. The Mac died once and took uncommitted work with it.

**Installing my own game on my own phone** ate more nights than any bug. A 408 MB install over Wi-Fi failed four times. One evening I accused the agent of lying about Wi-Fi speeds. 84 minutes later: *“it was low power mode on the phone try again”*.

# AI couldn’t make my ships. It made a lot of everything else.

This sub will care about this one. From April to October I tried to get AI to make the 3D ships: 114 Meshy generations by hand, then about 145 agent-hours of tools. It never hit the bar.

* **Spring, before any code:** 43 Meshy generations by hand in the browser. They looked fine in a prototype at a distance. That turned out to be the trap.
* **August:** agents wrote destroyers and carriers in Python from primitives. Deleted after two days: *“trash the ones you generated and all the work that went into generating them, it was so bad”*.
* **September:** Codex built a Blender “ship workshop” I drove from my phone, first rebuilding ships from one picture, then cleaning up Meshy text/image-to-3D models. **192 revisions across 26 ship projects, zero approved.** Shrinking a 3M-triangle Meshy model to a 2k phone budget turns hard edges into clay: *“holy cow meshy1 in rev6 is SO BAD”*.
* **October:** a fleet of Claude agents built a whole “ship compiler” with three AI judges in about 16 hours. The judges’ median went 4.5 → 5 → 5.5 → 5.5 → 5.5 and stopped. The real reference images scored \~8.5. The “big improvement” round made the fighter look like a bus.
* **Result:** 114 Meshy generations between April 29 and September 19. 7 reached the game, 6 were replaced, and 78 of the 90 hulls are bought Unity Asset Store packs.
* **What AI** ***did*** **ship:** 275 portraits and 65 icons (OpenAI image models), the app icon, the paint on my own ships, the 96 radio calls (ElevenLabs, after rejecting 663 and then 48) and 41 of 66 sound effects.

My takeaway: AI is great at making a picture of a ship and bad at making a ship. It worked when the output was 2D or audio, small, and judgeable in a second. It failed on hard-surface 3D that has to hold up from every angle at 2,000 triangles. The full write-up with the renders: [I tried to make AI build my spaceships](https://jamesktan.substack.com/p/i-tried-to-make-ai-build-my-spaceships)

# The dark factory (my biggest failure)

In October I tried to build a “lights-out” factory: agents build the game, play it, capture media, write store copy and submit to the stores, with nobody watching. The goal was to paste one prompt into any project and have it ship.

* A 49-agent run: 13.5M tokens in 3.1 hours, then the usage limit
* A 121-agent resume: 37.8M tokens, 11.6 hours unattended, died at my monthly spend limit
* Status report a week in: *“roughly 40%… none of it checked… none of it committed”*
* When I pushed Codex on the paste-in prompt: *“I presented the prompt as more complete than it was.”*

Total: **\~200 agents, 63M tokens, 348,000 lines of TypeScript, \~10,000 passing tests, and zero real store submissions.** Every store test ran against a fake store. I killed it and asked for “a straight path”. The straight path became a small release kit that got a test app onto an iPhone the same day, and it’s what ships my builds now.

Automation got exactly as far as its checks could see. Wherever the measure was taste, feel or a real store, a human had to close the loop.

# If I started again tomorrow

1. **Put the game on the real device on day one.** Never accept “fixed” without a screenshot from the screen the player touches.
2. **Write every decision down where the agents will read it**, the minute you make it. A handoff file plus short rule notes beats any amount of chat history.
3. **Make the agents build probes that photograph the game.** If an agent can’t see it, it will guess, and tell you the guess is a fact.
4. **Lock the nouns early.** I wrote 425 dialogue trees on top of names I changed three times.
5. **Tag a build you like** and put every new behavior behind a settings switch so you can A/B it.
6. **One integrator.** Parallel agents can edit. One lead builds, tests and commits.
7. **Don’t build the factory before you’ve shipped by hand.**
8. **Make them report in plain words.** What’s on the phone, what isn’t, a few sentences.

# The game

It’s called **Eimyrja: The Last Fleet**, an isometric space combat game. You wake with a damaged ship and no memory, the jump gates open for you after a century, and you fight your way home through the space of five peoples who each remember the Collapse differently.

* **Campaign:** 8 chapters, 26 systems, 42 missions, docks, refits, 110 castaways to rescue and a wing to recruit.
* **Single player:** Survival waves, missions on five hand-built faction maps, big two-sided Conflict battles, and the experimental Hunted mode (sneak through a fortress to its escape gate).
* **Co-op:** 2–4 pilots, 15 waves, online or local.

It’s out on the App Store for iPhone and iPad ($4.99, no ads, no in-app purchases), and Android is in progress: [https://apps.apple.com/us/app/eimyrja-the-last-fleet/id6816837471](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/eimyrja-the-last-fleet/id6816837471)

The long version, with all the charts, is here: [2,573 prompts later: the Eimyrja post-mortem](https://jamesktan.substack.com/p/2573-prompts-later-the-eimyrja-post). Happy to go deep on any of it in the comments.

**Question for you:** how are you handling the “the agent says it’s fixed” problem? Probes, screenshots in the loop, a second model as a checker, something else? That one cost me more than everything else combined.
